TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES AND THE PUBLIC
UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:

       Glenn Hodge, Ryan Hodge, Schwertner Farms, Inc., JT Carothers Holdings,
LLC, and MCP 18 LLC (together, the “Hodge-Schwertner Intervenors”) timely file
these Replies to Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision (“PFD”) issued August 20,
2026, pursuant to the Exceptions and Replies Memorandum filed the same date, which
sets September 9, 2026 as the deadline for replies to exceptions.1

                                          SUMMARY OF REPLIES
       Hodge-Schwertner Intervenors take no position on whether the Commission
should adopt the PFD’s recommendation to deny the Application. Should the
Commission approve the Application, it must still select a route, and the exceptions do
not supply a reason to approve a route using Link E12. Hodge-Schwertner Intervenors
continue to support Route 894 on the route-wide record developed below, however these
Replies focus on the narrower route-specific concern: the Commission should not
approve a route using Link E12. Hodge-Schwertner Intervenors therefore do not ask the
Commission to reject an otherwise supportable non-E12 route merely because it is not
Route 894.
        Four sets of exceptions directly seek routes that would reintroduce Link E12.
The Solana Intervenors, the Brady Creek Intervenors, and Staten Creek Ranch urge
Route 392, the only Focus Route that uses Link E12. Whitis urges “Whitis Route 1-14,”
which uses Links E11, E12, E7, and E8. Two further exceptions require narrower
treatment: 4K Land’s Northern Corridor slate includes Route 392 among numerous
alternatives, and Mr. Yates lists Route 392 as one of three routes he would accept.2

                                           ARGUMENT

                 I. INTRODUCTION AND SCOPE OF THESE REPLIES
        The PFD recommends that the Commission deny the Application because
Applicants did not comply with the public-meeting notice requirements of 16 TAC
§ 22.52(a)(4) as to approximately 1,400 later-affected landowners, and separately failed
to establish that Import Path 2 is necessary under PURA § 37.056. (PFD at 45–46, 98–
99.) The PFD further recommends that, should the Commission nevertheless approve
the Application, the Commission select Route 894, the route the Joint Applicants
identified as best meeting the Commission’s routing criteria and the route Hodge-
Schwertner Intervenors’ witness Brian C. Andrews independently recommended.11
       Hodge-Schwertner Intervenors did not brief Issues 5–7 (Need) in the proceedings
below and do not do so in these Replies. The Joint Applicants, Commission Staff,
Delaware Basin Midstream LLC, and other parties have presented full exceptions on
whether the PFD’s recommendation of denial should be sustained or reversed, and
Hodge-Schwertner Intervenors have nothing to add to that record that would assist the
Commission’s determination of Issues 1–7. Should the Commission reverse the PFD’s
recommendation of denial and approve the Application, however, the Commission
must still select a route, and these Replies address that question.12

PFD’s conditional selection of Route 894 and urge the Commission, if it approves the
Application, to select some other route instead, among them Route 296 (Carpenter Land

Burrow), Route 487 (Commission Staff and the J27, J25, J4 Opposition Landowners),
Route 891 (Jerome and Gaylynn Sneed), “Route 894 Western Modification 1” (Link R1
Opposition Landowners). Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve opposes Route 894 and

                         II. ROUTING CRITERIA (ISSUES 8–10)
A. Route 894 remains the best-supported route, and the exceptions do not establish
   a need to use E12.

Link E12 has 40; the median link has one habitable structure and the mean is 4.1. Those
counts use the same 500-foot centerline-buffer metric applied uniformly to every link and
route. That metric represents exposure measured by a uniform protocol, not an analytical
artifact. Route 894 avoids both outliers. Of the routes of interest, Route 392 is the only
one that uses Link E12.16 The route-level comparison confirms the link-level picture:

        Route 894 has fewer habitable structures than each of the other Focus Routes,
avoids both Salado-area outlier links, places no right-of-way within the Environmental
Assessment’s standardized park foreground-visual-zone metric, and remains the Joint
Applicants’ best-meets route and Mr. Andrews’s independent recommendation. Each
competing Focus Route improves some metrics only by accepting tradeoffs on others.
        Route 392 is worse than Route 894 on cost, habitable structures, and length, and
it is worse by the largest margin of any Focus Route on habitable structures: 51 more than
Route 894, a 60% increase. It is also the only Focus Route that takes that tradeoff by using
E12.17 Several exceptions read the ALJs’ description of their task as choosing the “least
bad option” as a signal that the Route 894 recommendation is weakly held. It is not.
        On a record in which no filed route is unopposed and every route imposes some
impact, comparative selection among imperfect alternatives is precisely what PURA §
37.056(c) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) require. The question is not whether Route 894
is without drawbacks, and Hodge-Schwertner Intervenors need not defend every one of
those drawbacks to protect their route-specific interest in avoiding Link E12.
        The PFD’s contingent recommendation is not based on habitable structure count
alone. The proposed findings state that Route 894 presents an appropriate overall balance
of routing factors; has 85 known habitable structures and complies with prudent
avoidance; adequately addresses expressed community values; uses or parallels existing
compatible rights-of-way to a reasonable extent in the total balance; crosses no park or
recreational area, has none within 1,000 feet, and has no right-of-way within the
Environmental Assessment’s half-mile park foreground visual zone; minimizes aesthetic
and historical/archaeological impacts to a reasonable extent; and presents an appropriate
balance between environmental integrity and the other routing considerations. The ALJs
then recommend Route 894 in Conclusion of Law 16. Many of the exceptions attack
selected components of the balance; they do not erase the full picture that led the ALJs to
the same route the Applicants identified as best addressing the Commission’s criteria.18
        The route alternatives further illustrate why isolated factor-by-factor criticisms do
not create a case for Link E12. Route 487 is modestly cheaper than Route 894 but has
more habitable structures and substantially more right-of-way within the Environmental
Assessment’s park foreground-zone metric. Route 410 reaches U3 and performs strongly
on the hard-infrastructure paralleling measures emphasized by Northern Corridor

B. The hearing record’s ground-level testimony confirms that Link E12
   concentrates existing, avoidable impacts that a bare structure count does not
   capture.

        Before addressing the Solana, Brady Creek, Staten Creek, and Whitis Exceptions
individually, it bears emphasis that the 51-to-55-structure differential separating Route
894 from Route 392 and Whitis Route 1-14 is not an abstraction. Save Our Salado
(“SOS”), an unrepresented group of more than 70 intervenors along Link E12 appearing
pro se with limited-scope administrative assistance from the undersigned counsel,
presented unrebutted testimony at hearing identifying specific existing homes and uses
that Link E12 would affect. That testimony is already part of the record these Replies ask
the Commission to weigh, and it directly answers the Solana, Brady Creek, and Whitis
Exceptions’ shared premise that a habitable-structure differential of this size can be
dismissed as merely statistical or discounted as “numerically insignificant” or offset
against a modest cost savings.20
        The SOS record shows that Link E12 would run within yards of existing homes
and other existing uses, not through an empty corridor. Craig and Carleen Edwards’
primary bedroom, guest bedroom, and patio sit 98 feet from the proposed E12 easement;
their home does not appear on Applicants’ habitable-structure list despite their having
lived there for nearly a year. They survived the November 2018 Camp Fire in Paradise,
California, which was a fire caused by a worn, broken hook on a transmission-tower that
destroyed their home and town, burned approximately 153,336 acres, destroyed 18,804
structures, and killed 85 people. The Camp Fire was among the wildfires for which the

        The SOS record also identifies institutional and historic resources concentrated

2,000 feet of a new high school built as part of a $270 million bond voters approved in
2023; he asks the Commission to select a route other than E12 or E13.
         Larry Rosamond, testifying for Misstex Investments, LLC, describes an 86-lot
residential subdivision already more than 90% built out, with an additional 261 residential
lots, 84 townhome lots, and 10 commercial lots engineered and pending approval; Link
E12 runs through the subdivision’s western section, rendering that portion “effectively
worthless” and making homes backing to the line “almost unsellable.” And Bree Carrico
testifies that the Historic Stagecoach Inn, in continuous operation since 1860, the second-
oldest inn or hotel in Texas, sitting on the Chisholm Trail and host to historical figures
including Sam Houston and Jesse James, would sit within sight of 160-to-190-foot lattice

Texas.22
